en: The Jātaka:
The Fortieth Collection (Cattālīsanipāta), The Chapter on the Teṃsakūṇa Birds (Tesakuṇavagga)
2. The Sarabhaṅga Jātaka:
“Adorned with earrings, well-dressed, with necklaces of beryl and pearls, and girdles bound with sword-hilts;”
“O bull among charioteers, stand still!
Who are you, and how are you known in the world of men?
“I am Aṭṭhaka, and this one here is Bhīmaratha.”
"But the King of Kaliṅga is fierce and violent;
we have come here to see the well-restrained seers and have asked them these questions."
“You stand in the air, in the midst of the sky,
like the full moon on the fifteenth day.
I ask you, O powerful yakṣa:”
"How do they know him in the world of men?
"Among the gods they call him Sujampati;
in the world of men they call him Maghava."
That king of the gods has arrived today to behold these sages who are so well-restrained.
We have heard from afar that the sages have assembled here.
Possessed of great psychic power and endowed with the qualities of supernormal success,
I pay homage to you, O Noble One, with a heart full of faith—
to those who are the best among men here in the world of the living.
“The fragrance of seers who have long been ordained,
having departed from the body, travels with the wind;
turning back from here, O thousand-eyed one, [do not approach].”
“The odor of the seers is impure, O King of Devas.
“Let the odor of the seers who have long been consecrated,
having departed from their bodies, go away with the wind.”
“O Bhante, we expect this to be like a fragrant garland of various flowers and a sweet scent; for here,
the devas do not perceive it as repulsive.”
“Purindada, Lord of Beings, the Glorious One,
Sakka, Maghavan, Sujampati— this king of the gods,
the crusher of the hosts of asuras.”
He seeks an opportunity to ask a question:
"Who here among these wise ones will explain these subtle questions when he is asked?"
And of three kings who were lords of men,
and of Vāsava, the lord of the gods.
“This seer Sarabhaṅga is an ascetic;”
“Since he was born, he has abstained from sexual intercourse;
the son of a teacher, well-disciplined in appearance,
he will answer their questions.”
“Koṇḍañña, answer these questions;
the seers of noble form entreat you.
Koṇḍañña, this is the Dhamma among men.”
"That which comes with growth— this is the burden.
"May the venerable ones ask whatever question they desire in their minds, having been granted leave."
"For I shall answer each of you,
having known for myself this world and the next.
Then Maghavā Sakka—
Atthadassī, the Giver of Wealth in the Beginning,
asked the first question,
that which he had long desired.
“Having slain what does one never grieve?
What do the seers praise as the thing to be abandoned?
Whose harsh speech here should one endure?”
“Tell me this matter, Koṇḍañña.
“Having slain anger, one never grieves;
the seers praise the abandonment of hypocrisy.”
“Forgive the harsh words spoken by everyone;
the virtuous call this the highest patience.
“It is possible to endure the speech of both parties.”
“Whether it be from an equal or even from one superior,
how indeed could one endure the speech of an inferior?
Explain this matter to me, Koṇḍañña.”
One might indeed endure the words of a superior out of fear,
or those of an equal out of a desire for confrontation;
but he who here endures the words of an inferior— [he is truly patient].
“The virtuous call this patience supreme.
“How should one know the fourfold spread-out form—
whether it be excellent, similar, or inferior?”
The virtuous move about in various forms;
therefore, one should endure the words of all.
For even a vast army does not achieve this purpose.
Even kings engaged in battle might obtain [victory],
but what a patient and virtuous person obtains is this:
through patience, the enmities of the powerful are stilled.
“Rejoicing in what you have well spoken, I ask you another question; please tell me this:
how did Daṇḍakī Nāḷikera come to be?”
Now, tell me the destination of Ajuna and King Kalabu— those of very evil deeds—
who were the harassers of the seers; where have they been reborn?
“Why indeed, Vaccha, does one who wields a staff, having cast aside his kin,
with roots cut off and abandoned by his country,
boil in the hell named Kukkuḷa?”
Sparks fall upon his body—
he who harms a restrained renunciant,
a blameless ascetic while he is preaching the Dhamma.
Then dogs gather together and devour that coconut while it is still quivering.
Then Ajuna [falls] into the hell of spears and spikes.
Falling head-first with feet upwards,
having insulted Gotama of the Aṅgīrasa clan—
the patient ascetic who has long practiced the holy life.
He who had the one gone forth cut into pieces—
that harmless ascetic who spoke only of patience—
was reborn in the Kalābu-vīci hell and is there tormented.
Having heard of these hells— Mahāpatāpa, Kaṭuka,
and Bhayānaka— the wise person [should also consider] others that are even more terrible still.
One should practice the Dhamma among recluses and brahmins;
acting thus, one goes to a heavenly state.
Rejoicing in what you have well-spoken, [I say this].
I ask you another thing; please tell me this:
what kind of person do they call virtuous, and what kind of person do they call wise?
"What kind of person do they call a true man?
What kind of person does glory never forsake?
"He who is restrained in body and in speech..."
One does no evil even with the mind,
nor does one speak falsehood for one's own sake;
such a person they call virtuous.
Reflecting with the mind upon a profound question,
one does not perform harmful or cruel deeds;
one does not neglect the timely arrival of a meaningful opportunity.
They call one such as this "possessed of wisdom.
Indeed, he who is grateful and appreciative, wise,
a friend of virtue, and firm in devotion;
One who respectfully performs the duties for one who is suffering—
such a person they call a true man (sappurisa).
One who is endowed with all these virtues...
The person who is faithful, gentle, generous,
and charitable; who is inclusive, friendly, and soft-spoken—
glory does not forsake such a one as this.
“Rejoicing in what you have well-spoken, I ask you another thing; pray tell me this:
regarding virtue, glory, and the Dhamma of the virtuous,”
"And they declare wisdom to be the most excellent. "For the wise say that wisdom is supreme,
like the king of stars among the constellations."
“Virtue, glory, and the Dhamma of the good—
these follow after one who possesses wisdom.
Having rejoiced in your well-spoken words, [I say:]
I ask you another thing; please tell me this:
By doing what, by performing what, by practicing what, and by associating with whom, does one obtain wisdom in this world?
Now, tell me the path for wisdom:
how does a mortal become wise?
"One should serve those who are mature, skillful, and learned."
One should be a grasper of the teachings and an inquirer;
one should listen attentively to well-spoken words.
Acting in this way, a mortal becomes wise.
The wise one examines the strands of sensual pleasure as impermanent,
as suffering, and as a disease;
thus seeing clearly, he abandons desire.
Toward sensual pleasures, which are full of suffering and great danger,
he who is free from passion should cast out hatred and cultivate a measureless mind of loving-kindness.
“Having laid aside the rod toward all beings,
blameless, he attains the Brahma state.
“Your coming has been for a great purpose;”
“Tava-m-aṭṭhaka, Bhīmaratha,
and the exalted King of Kaliṅga— for all of you,
sensual desire has been abandoned.”
“Thus it is that you know the minds of others;
in all of us, sensual lust has been abandoned.
Grant us the opportunity to show you favor.”
"So that we may attain the same state as you.
"I grant you leave out of compassion,
for indeed your passion for sensual pleasures has been abandoned."
“Pharātha kāyaṁ with abundant rapture,
so that I may attain my destination. “We shall do everything according to your instruction.”
Whatever you shall speak, O one of vast wisdom,
may it pervade our bodies with abundant joy,
so that we may attain the same destination as you.
“Vatsa has been honored, though he is emaciated;
let the worthy seers depart.
Be always delighted in meditation and ever composed.”
“This is the supreme delight for one who has gone forth.
Having heard these verses, which were endowed with the ultimate meaning and well-spoken by the wise sage, [he was moved].
Rejoicing, those gods born of the Vedas,
glorious ones, departed for the city of the gods.
These verses are meaningful and well-phrased.
These well-spoken words were uttered by the Sage, the Wise One;
whoever listens to them with earnest intent will obtain distinction between what precedes and what follows.
Having attained distinction between what precedes and what follows,
one should go to the non-perception of the King of Death.
“Sāriputta is the essence of the Sālis.”
Meṇḍissara and Kassapa;
Pabbata and Anuruddha,
and Kaccāyana and Devala.
Anusissa and Ānanda,
Kisavaccha and Kolita;
Nārada and the Elder Udāyī—
“The assembly is the assembly of Buddhas;
Sarabhaṅga is the Lord of the World—
thus you should remember this Jātaka.”
The Second Jātaka: The Story of Sarabhaṅga.
